name: Yaoyao lingxian (遥遥领先)
blurb: "Far, far ahead": a tech-keynote boast turned into an all-purpose Chinese joke in 2023
title: Yaoyao Lingxian (遥遥领先) Meme: Meaning, Origin & Trend
description: 遥遥领先 ("far, far ahead") is a phrase Huawei executive Richard Yu often used at launch events. In 2023 it became a meme for boasts and teasing.
h1: What is the 遥遥领先 (yaoyao lingxian) meme?
answer: 遥遥领先 (yáoyáo lǐngxiān) literally means "far, far ahead". It became a meme because Richard Yu (余承东), a Huawei executive, used it repeatedly in product keynotes; media counted 14 uses at one October 2020 launch. In late August 2023 netizens took it up as a catchphrase, both to praise technology and to tease an over-the-top speaking style, and the weekly 语言文字周报 named it one of its top ten internet buzzwords of 2023.

body: On its own the phrase is ordinary Chinese for being well ahead of competitors. The meme is about delivery: a keynote speaker stressing "far ahead" again and again, which fans clipped together into compilations. Netizens then started saying it about anything, sincerely or not.
A news report summarising the 2023 buzzword list put both sides plainly: the phrase is used to praise technical innovation, and also to gently mock an exaggerated way of talking.

head: Date
Event

ul: Self-teasing: "My ability to procrastinate is 遥遥领先."
Praise in comments: "This team's defence? 遥遥领先."
Mock-keynote style: listing trivial things and calling each one "far ahead"
"先遥遥领先一下": jokingly claiming victory before anything has happened

body: The peak was autumn and winter 2023. The phrase is now a recognisable piece of Chinese internet vocabulary for boasting or ironic praise, used well beyond technology. Its tone depends on context: it can be sincere admiration, friendly teasing or sarcasm.

faq.q: What does 遥遥领先 mean in English?
faq.a: "Far, far ahead" or "way ahead of the rest".

faq.q: Who made 遥遥领先 famous?
faq.a: Richard Yu (余承东), a Huawei executive, who used it often in launch keynotes. Netizens turned it into a meme in 2023.
Both. It is used to praise, to brag jokingly about yourself, and to tease exaggerated claims.
